verses.1:2: {v2a}, * e na sua lei meditará dia e noite.
verses.1:3a: E será como {lignum} junto {decursus}, * que dará o seu fruto no seu tempo:
verses.1:3b: E a sua folha não cairá: * e todas as coisas que fizer prosperarão.
verses.1:4: {nonsic}: * mas como o pó que o vento {proicit} da face da terra.
verses.1:5: Por isso os ímpios não {resurgent} no juízo: * nem os pecadores {concilio} dos justos.
verses.1:6: Porque o Senhor conhece o caminho dos justos: * e {iter} dos ímpios perecerá.

decisions.why: The first word of the psalter, and a word said 29 times in it (grep of the DO Latin: Beátus vir 1:1, 31:2, 33:9, 39:5, 83:6, 111:1, 126:5; Beáti 2:13, 31:1, 83:5, 105:3, 118:1–2, 127:1; beátus pópulus, beáta gens, beátum dixérunt, beátum fáciat eum 40:3 …). Ps 1 and Ps 2 are framed by it (1:1 Beátus vir … 2:13 beáti omnes), so whatever is chosen is said again at the end of the next psalm. The glossary has 'bem-aventurado o homem' as working; Ps 118:1–2 is already translated 'Bem-aventurados'. The real rival is 'feliz' (the Diurnal Monástico 1962, from the Hebrew), and D2 gives the ear 'the plainer of two faithful words' — so the question is whether 'feliz' is a faithful word for beátus. Lewis & Short: 'happy, prosperous, blessed, fortunate', with Cicero's definition 'secretis malis omnibus, cumulata bonorum complexio' — a state pronounced over someone, not a feeling he has. The Latin psalter never uses felix (grep: no form of it), so beátus (μακάριος) is its one word for this.

options.label: Bem-aventurado
options.note: Ruling, with the glossary, Matos Soares 1932 (1:1 and 2:13 in the parallels) and this project's own Ps 118:1–2. Reasons: (1) 'feliz' today is first a mood — 'estou feliz' — and 'Feliz o homem que…' is heard as 'the man who … is glad', where beátus is a verdict on a life (Cicero's definition above); 'bem-aventurado' can only be the verdict. (2) It is the one Portuguese word that is heard as a macarism: the reader crossing from 'Beátus' / 'Beáti' needs a word that sounds like a formula, since the Latin word is one — 29 times, nearly always first in its verse. (3) It works in every construction the psalter has: 143:15 'Beátum dixérunt pópulum' → 'chamaram bem-aventurado o povo', 40:3 'beátum fáciat eum' → 'o faça bem-aventurado', 127:2 'beátus es'. (4) It is not an archaism needing a footnote: everyone who prays knows it — neither blind reader remarked on it, and the stylist passed the opening. Cost, not hidden: five syllables for three (Bem-aventurado o homem: 8 against Beátus vir: 4). It falls at the head of the verse, on the reciting note, where length is cheapest; in 1:1 the first colon still comes within two syllables of the Latin. That the Beatitudes are 'Bem-aventurados' in Portuguese is common knowledge but was not fetched tonight: unverified, and not needed for the ruling.

options.label: Feliz
options.note: DM1962 ('FELIZ o homem que não segue…') — made from the Hebrew, but a witness of what Brazilian monks actually prayed, and the word of the current Brazilian liturgical psalter as far as I know (unverified). Plain, two syllables, oxytone, exactly the Latin's length ('Feliz o homem': 4–5). Lexically inside beátus (L&S 'happy'). Refused as the text because it names the feeling before the state, and because across 29 places it would make the psalter's one solemn formula sound like a greeting-card word; but it is the option Gustavo should weigh most seriously, since it is the plainer word and D2 leans to the plainer word.

options.label: Ditoso
options.note: Three syllables, paroxytone, means 'fortunate, blessed by lot' — close to beátus and the right length. Literary and faintly old-fashioned (rule 5: no poeticism); nobody prays it.

decisions.why: The Latin says vir (ἀνήρ), the male, not homo (ἄνθρωπος) — and the psalter has both macarisms: Beátus vir seven times, Beátus homo twice (83:13, 93:12). Portuguese has one plain word, 'homem', for both, and one marked word, 'varão', for vir alone. The ambiguity reader heard 'o homem' as 'anyone' first and 'a male' second — which is how vir is prayed too.

options.label: homem
options.note: Ruling, with the glossary, Matos Soares 1932 and DM1962. The plainer of two faithful words (D2): 'homem' is both vir and homo in living Portuguese, and in 'o homem que…' it is heard as the particular man, as vir is. Cost: Beátus vir and Beátus homo become one phrase — accepted, since no verse sets the two side by side as a contrast (the two 'Beátus homo' verses stand alone).

options.label: varão
options.note: Keeps vir apart from homo, and is oxytone. It is a word of old Bibles and of registry offices ('filho varão'); in prayer today it sounds archaic and draws attention to itself in the first line of the psalter (rule 5). If Gustavo ever wants vir / homo kept apart psalter-wide, this is the word.

decisions.why: abíre is 'to go off, go away'; with 'in consílio' (ablative) the Latin is a stiff calque of the Greek ἐπορεύθη ἐν βουλῇ, 'walked in the counsel' (Douay-Rheims: 'hath not walked in the counsel'). The psalm sets three verbs of the body in a row — went, stood, sat — and the three must stay three. The glossary has ambuláre → andar, and the Greek verb here is the same one that stands behind 118:1 'qui ámbulant in lege Dómini' (πορεύομαι), already translated 'os que andam na lei do Senhor'. The ambiguity reader heard 'andou no conselho dos ímpios' first as 'followed the advice of the wicked' and second as 'frequented a council of the wicked': consílium is both, so the Portuguese is as open as the Latin.

options.label: andou no conselho
options.note: Ruling. 'Andar no conselho de' is as odd and as clear in Portuguese as 'abíre in consílio' is in Latin — the counsel is a place one walks in, which prepares the 'way' and the 'chair' — and it makes this verse answer 118:1 (not in the counsel of the wicked / in the law of the Lord), as it does in the Greek. Cost: abíre and ambuláre share a verb; the ab- ('away') goes unheard, as it does in Douay-Rheims. The stylist would put the verb last here too ('que no conselho dos ímpios não andou'), so that the flex does not fall on 'ímpios', which he hears as proparoxytone; refused: the Latin's first colon is verb-first, 'ímpios' is two syllables in Brazilian speech (ím-pios, paroxytone — so checks.py), and it closes cola again in 1:4 and nowhere can it be avoided.

options.label: se foi no conselho
options.note: Hugs ab-íre, 'went off'. 'Que não se foi no conselho dos ímpios' is hard to parse at sight: 'ir-se' wants a 'from' or a 'to', and the bare 'foi' is also 'was'.

options.label: seguiu o conselho
options.note: DM1962 ('não segue o conselho'; Matos Soares 1932 goes further: 'não se deixou levar pelo conselho'). Natural, but it turns the counsel from a place one walks in into advice one takes, and loses the first of the three postures. Refused under D2: an image paraphrased.

decisions.latin: et in via peccatórum non stetit … et in cáthedra pestiléntiæ non sedit
decisions.why: Two things at once, because they share the slots. (1) The word for stetit: stare is 'to stand' and also 'to stand still, stay' (L&S); the glossary has stare → 'estar de pé' (open, Ps 133:1b), which suits a man standing in God's house but not one on a road. (2) The order: the Latin is verb-first in the first colon and verb-last in the next two (non ábiit in… / in via… non stetit / in cáthedra… non sedit). D2 gives order to the ear; but a fronted complement is ordinary elevated Portuguese, and the verb-last pair lets the hearer follow the Latin column word for word. Draft 1 had 'não parou, * … não se sentou'; the stylist named the verse the worst of the psalm, chiefly for that rhyme ('muito audível entre a mediana e o final').

options.label: e no caminho dos pecadores não se deteve, * e na {cathedra} não se sentou

forms.v1b: e no caminho dos pecadores não se deteve

options.note: Draft 2: Matos Soares 1932's verb ('não se deteve no caminho dos pecadores'), asked for by the stylist. 'Deter-se' is to stop and stay, which is stetit on a road; the mediant now closes paroxytone and the rhyme with 'sentou' is gone. In draft 1 I kept 'parou' on the ground that the Latin has the same echo (stetit / sedit) — but the Latin's echo is of two unstressed endings, and an oxytone rhyme on the very syllable the tone lands on is a much louder thing; the stylist's ear is right. Both verbs are faithful, so this is a change of how, not of what (D2). The Latin's order is kept in both cola.

options.label: e no caminho dos pecadores não parou, * e na {cathedra} não se sentou

forms.v1b: e no caminho dos pecadores não parou

options.note: Draft 1. 'Parar' is the plainest word for what a walker does when he stands still: andou / parou / sentou-se. The three verbs end alike, and the last two rhyme at the mediant and the final.

options.label: e não se deteve no caminho dos pecadores, * e não se sentou na {cathedra}

forms.v1b: e não se deteve no caminho dos pecadores

options.note: Everyday order, three cola built alike. Closes on 'pecadores' and 'pestilência', both paroxytone. Flatter; the Latin's turn from verb-first to verb-last is lost.

options.label: … não se deteve, * e na {cathedra} não tomou assento

forms.v1b: e no caminho dos pecadores não se deteve

options.note: The stylist's close. Refused: 'tomar assento' is a ceremonious periphrasis for the plainest verb in the verse (sedit), and once 'se deteve' stands at the mediant there is no rhyme left for it to cure.

options.label: e no caminho dos pecadores não esteve de pé, * e na {cathedra} não se sentou

forms.v1b: e no caminho dos pecadores não esteve de pé

options.note: The glossary's 'estar de pé' for stare (Ps 133:1b). Keeps the posture as a posture; but 'estar de pé no caminho' is a man standing on a road, not one who has stopped on it, and the colon runs four syllables over.

decisions.why: A Septuagintal reading to be kept (rule 1): the Greek has ἐπὶ καθέδραν λοιμῶν, 'on the seat of the pestilent', where the Hebrew has the seat of the scoffers (DM1962: 'na assembléia dos que zombam'). The Latin turns the Greek's plural persons into an abstract genitive, pestiléntiæ — 'the chair of pestilence' (Douay-Rheims) — and that is the image to keep: a chair (cáthedra is the seat one teaches or presides from; 106:32 'in cáthedra seniórum') and a contagion. L&S lists this very phrase under the figurative sense of pestiléntia. The ambiguity reader heard the image rightly first ('a place of corruption or harmful moral influence'), a literally infected chair second, and listed 'pestilência' as a word some will not know.

options.label: cadeira da pestilência
options.note: Ruling. 'Cadeira' is the plain word and also the teacher's chair in Portuguese; 'pestilência' is the cognate, kept apart from pestis, and transparent to anyone who knows 'peste'. With the article the pestilence is a power that has a chair, as the Latin's bare genitive allows. The image is given and not explained (Matos Soares 1932 adds '(dos maus)'). Latinist and stylist both passed it.

options.label: cadeira de pestilência
options.note: Genitive of quality — a pestilent chair — which is what stands behind the Latin historically. Without the article it sounds like a kind of furniture ('cadeira de balanço').

options.label: cadeira pestilencial
options.note: Matos Soares 1932. The same reading as the option above, with an adjective for the Latin's noun.

options.label: cadeira da peste
options.note: Answers the ambiguity reader's 'unknown word': everyone knows 'peste', and L&S glosses pestiléntia 'a plague, pest'. But 'peste' in Brazil is also a mild insult, the phrase turns faintly comic, and the Latin has pestis as a separate word to keep free.

options.label: cátedra da pestilência
options.note: The cognate; says 'teaching chair' unmistakably, which is how the Fathers read the verse. Learned and proparoxytone; 'cadeira' already carries the sense.

decisions.latin: Sed in lege Dómini volúntas ejus
decisions.why: Draft 1 kept the Latin's order, 'Mas na lei do Senhor está a sua vontade'. The ambiguity reader heard it first as 'the Lord's will is expressed in his law' — 'pela proximidade entre Senhor e sua' — and only second as the man's will being set on the law. In form the Latin's ejus is just as open; but no one praying the Latin takes it so, because volúntas ejus … in lege ejus sorts itself (his will / His law), while in Portuguese the wrong reading came first. The case is the same as 53:8, where a vocative was moved for the same reason: the Latin's words are all kept and only the order yields (D2).

options.label: Mas a sua vontade está na lei do Senhor

forms.v2a: Mas a sua vontade está na lei do Senhor

options.note: Draft 2. 'A sua vontade' now comes before the Lord is named, so it attaches to the man of 1:1, and 'na sua lei' in the next colon falls right after 'do Senhor', whose law it is. It is the order of Douay-Rheims ('But his will is in the law of the Lord'); Matos Soares 1932 has the same sequence ('tem a sua vontade posta na lei do Senhor'). The mediant closes on 'Senhor', oxytone. Cost: the Latin's anaphora (in lege Dómini … in lege ejus, both cola opening alike) becomes a chiasm (… na lei do Senhor, * e na sua lei …) — the two 'lei' still stand, and now side by side. 'Está' is the copula Portuguese needs; the Latin has none.

options.label: Mas na lei do Senhor está a sua vontade

forms.v2a: Mas na lei do Senhor está a sua vontade

options.note: Draft 1: the Latin's order, both cola opening on 'na lei'. Heard by the blind reader as the Lord's will first.

decisions.why: lignum is 'wood' and, by a Septuagintalism (ξύλον), 'tree'; the Latin did not write arbor. Christian reading has heard the wood of the Cross in it for that reason. Portuguese 'lenho' is the matching word — wood, and in church speech the Cross ('o lenho da cruz') — but a 'lenho' cannot be planted or bear leaves.

options.label: a árvore que foi plantada
options.note: Ruling, with Douay-Rheims ('a tree which is planted') and Matos Soares 1932 ('a árvore, que está plantada'). What lignum means here; the plainer of two faithful words. The definite article follows the Greek (τὸ ξύλον), which the Latin cannot show. The relative clause is kept ('que foi plantada … que dará'), because the Latin builds the verse on its two quod.

options.label: o lenho que foi plantado
options.note: The Latin's own word, with the Cross audible in it. In Portuguese a 'lenho' is a log: planted, fruiting and in leaf, it is a riddle, where the Latin is merely biblical.

options.label: uma árvore plantada
options.note: What a Brazilian would say unprompted (DM1962: 'como a árvore plantada'). Drops the first of the two relative clauses.

decisions.why: decúrsus is a running-down, a downward course (L&S cites this verse under the concrete sense, 'a descending aqueduct'); the Greek has διεξόδους, channels or outlets. Plural in both. Two nouns in the Latin, and both should be heard.

options.label: aos cursos de água
options.note: Draft 2, from the stylist: 'curso de água' is the living Portuguese for a watercourse, and 'cursos das águas', with the article, 'soa traduzida'. Both of the Latin's nouns are still heard and decúrsus keeps its plural; only aquárum loses its number, inside a fixed idiom — how the thing is said, not what (D2). In the mouth it is a syllable shorter (de‿água elides), though the checker, which does not elide, still counts the colon +3. Where the waters are the point (28:3 super aquas multas, 41:2 ad fontes aquárum) the plural will stand.

options.label: aos cursos das águas
options.note: Draft 1. The Latin's genitive plural kept; the stylist heard a translation.

options.label: às correntes das águas
options.note: Matos Soares 1932; Douay-Rheims 'running waters'. Good and known; 'correntes' is first the flow rather than the channel, and is also 'chains'.

decisions.why: The Latin (with the Greek: οὐχ οὕτως οἱ ἀσεβεῖς, οὐχ οὕτως) has no verb, and says 'non sic' twice. The stylist heard the verbless opening as 'um decalque perceptível da ordem latina' and asked for a copula in both halves. D2 lets a copula be supplied where Portuguese needs one; the question is whether it needs one here.

options.label: Não assim os ímpios, não assim

forms.nonsic: Não assim os ímpios, não assim

options.note: Draft, kept. The ellipsis is a figure, not a gap: an exclamation, as abrupt in Latin as in Portuguese. Both Portuguese antecedents print exactly these words — Matos Soares 1932 ('Não assim os ímpios, não assim') and the Diurnal Monástico 1962, which Brazilian monks prayed ('Não assim os maus, não assim') — so it is proven sayable. With two copulas the colon goes to 11 syllables against the Latin's 7 and the hammer-blow of the repeated 'non sic' is softened.

options.label: Não são assim os ímpios, não são assim

forms.nonsic: Não são assim os ímpios, não são assim

options.note: Stylist. Ordinary grammar, nothing of the Latin's words lost; four syllables over and slower.

decisions.latin: quem próicit ventus a fácie terræ
decisions.why: proícere is 'to throw forth, cast away'. It comes back at once in 2:3 (projiciámus a nobis jugum ipsórum) and in much-prayed verses: 50:13 Ne proícias me a fácie tua, 70:9, 76:8. So it wants one verb that takes a 'from'. Douay-Rheims has 'driveth from', Matos Soares 1932 'dispersa' (which is another verb, dispérgere).

options.label: lança
options.note: Ruling, and proposed for the glossary: proícere → lançar (de). Plain, takes 'de' naturally, and serves the other places: 2:3 'lancemos de nós o seu jugo', 50:13 'Não me lanceis da vossa face'. 'Lançai' would be safe under rule 3 (past 'lancei'). No reader remarked on it.

options.label: arremessa
options.note: Stronger and nearer the violence of pro-jícere; four syllables, and it does not sit well in 50:13.

options.label: varre
options.note: What wind does to dust in Portuguese; but it is a broom's verb, another image than throwing.

decisions.why: The Latin follows the Greek ἀναστήσονται and says 'rise again' — the verb of the resurrection — where the Hebrew has 'stand' (DM1962: 'Não ficarão de pé no julgamento'). Rule 1: the Latin's reading is kept, and its openness with it (whether the wicked will not rise at all, or will not rise 'in the judgment' to stand acquitted, the Latin does not say). The ambiguity reader heard 'will not come back to life at the Last Judgment' first and 'will not reappear / stand up at the judgment' second: the Latin's two readings, in the Latin's order of likelihood (Matos Soares 1932 glosses it the first way in a footnote).

options.label: ressurgirão
options.note: Ruling. The cognate of re-súrgere, current in Portuguese; Douay-Rheims 'shall not rise again'. Wide enough for both readings.

options.label: ressuscitarão
options.note: Matos Soares 1932. The everyday verb for rising from the dead; it is resuscitáre's word, which the psalter has as a verb of its own (40:11 resúscita me), and it narrows the verse to the general resurrection only.

options.label: se levantarão
options.note: The plain verb, without the 're-'; it is the Hebrew's sense ('stand up') rather than the Latin's, and 'levantar-se' already serves exsúrgere and insúrgere in the glossary.

decisions.why: The Greek has βουλῇ in 1:1 and again here; the Latin writes consílio there and concílio here — two words one letter apart. concílium recurs three times (21:17 concílium malignántium, 25:4 cum concílio vanitátis, 39:11 a concílio multo), and the psalter has a crowd of assembly-words that will each want a word of its own (ecclésia, synagóga, congregátio, convéntus, cœtus). Draft 1 had the cognate 'concílio', for the echo with 'conselho' in 1:1. Both blind readers stopped at it: the stylist ('evoca imediatamente uma reunião de bispos e exige recuperar um sentido mais amplo') and the ambiguity reader, who listed it among the words a hearer may not know.

options.label: na assembleia
options.note: Draft 2, from the stylist; DM1962's word. It is what concílium means, and the plainer of two faithful words (D2) — and the precedent of this project is that a word which fails both blind readers goes (opróbrio, Ps 118). Costs, for whoever rules on the glossary row: (1) the Latin's echo consílio / concílio is no longer heard; (2) 'assembleia' is also the natural word for ecclésia, and Ps 21 has both (21:17 concílium malignántium, 21:23 and 21:26 in ecclésia) — that psalm will have to move one of them.

options.label: no concílio
options.note: Draft 1. The cognate keeps the Latin's echo (conselho dos ímpios … concílio dos justos) and leaves 'assembleia' free for ecclésia. In Brazil 'concílio' is first of all a council of bishops; both blind readers stumbled.

options.label: na congregação
options.note: Matos Soares 1932. It is congregátio's cognate (the psalter has the word), and in Brazil a religious institute.

decisions.why: The Greek (ὁδός) and the Hebrew repeat one word; the Latin varies it: via for the just, iter for the wicked. Douay-Rheims and Matos Soares 1932 both go back to one word ('way … way', 'caminho … caminho'). D15 met the same question for verbum / sermo and ruled for one Portuguese word, because the variation carries no difference of sense and Portuguese had no plain second word — adding that verses which set the two side by side decide locally. Draft 1 kept the variation with 'a senda', on the ground that it cost the ear nothing. It did: the stylist found 'senda' literary against the plain speech of the rest and asked for 'caminho', and the ambiguity reader listed 'senda' as a word the hearer may not know ('se o ouvinte compreender senda').

options.label: o caminho
options.note: Draft 2, from the stylist; Douay-Rheims, Matos Soares 1932, and what the Greek says. D15's reasoning applied: a variation that is only the Latin translator's elegance yields when Portuguese has no second word that is equally plain. The psalm now closes on its theme-word said twice — the two ways. Cost: the reader crossing columns finds one word under via and iter. Glossary: iter → caminho (its other five places, 49:23, 67:5, 67:20, 79:10, 139:6, none beside via).

options.label: a senda
options.note: Draft 1. Two words where the Latin has two; 'senda' is free in the glossary (sémita took 'vereda'). Failed both blind readers as too literary.

options.label: a estrada
options.note: DM1962 uses 'estrada' in 1:1 for the sinners' way. Plain, but a built road; 'a estrada dos ímpios perecerá' is heard as a road being destroyed.

choices.1:1: The three genitives stay distinct, as the glossary has them: ímpii → ímpios, peccatóres → pecadores (and 1:5–6 justi → justos). consílium → conselho (as Ps 118:24), via → caminho (D15). The verse ends on a colon, as the Latin does, because 1:2 continues the sentence. First colon +2 by the checker, the price of 'Bem-aventurado'. DM1962 has this psalm (monastic Prime): it was heard for diction only — it reads the Hebrew ('dos que zombam') and says 'Feliz'.
choices.1:2: The Latin has no verb in the first colon; 'está' is the copula Portuguese needs (D2). volúntas → 'vontade', the Latin's word (Douay-Rheims 'his will is in the law'), not the Hebrew's 'delight' (DM1962 'se compraz'). Draft 2 takes the natural order in the first colon (decision 'v2order'). lex → lei, meditári → meditar em (D15; words/ps118-terms.md §5): 'na sua lei meditará' is the vocabulary of 118:16 'Nos vossos preceitos meditarei'. The future is kept (meditábitur; Matos Soares 1932 makes it a present). die ac nocte → 'dia e noite', the living phrase. The ambiguity reader asked whether it is the man or the Lord who meditates: he heard the man, rightly.
choices.1:3a: 'E será': the subject stays in the verb ending, as in the Latin; the man of 1:1–2 is still in the ear. fructum suum … in témpore suo: both possessives kept ('o seu fruto no seu tempo'); Matos Soares' idiom 'a seu tempo' is the alternative and drops the preposition 'in'. The ambiguity reader asked whose time — the tree's season or the man's moment: suo is as open, and he heard the tree's first. The verse ends on a colon as the Latin does.
choices.1:3b: The stylist's best line. fólium ejus → 'a sua folha', singular as in the Latin. défluet → 'cairá' (Douay-Rheims 'fall off', Matos Soares 1932 'cairá'), not 'murchará', which is the Hebrew's verb. ómnia quæcúmque → 'todas as coisas que' in the plural, so that the verse closes on 'prosperarão' and not on 'prosperará', which would rhyme with 'cairá' at the mediant where the Latin has no echo (rule 5). prosperabúntur is passive ('shall be prospered'); Portuguese 'prosperar' is already intransitive, so the passive is grammar that yields (D2); the glossary's 'fazer prosperar' (117:25) is the active of the same verb. Who 'does' — the man or the tree — is left as open as in the Latin. The ambiguity reader heard a shade of material success in 'prosperarão': prosperári has it too.
choices.1:4: 'Non sic … non sic' repeated as in the Latin (the second 'non sic' is the Greek's plus, not in the Hebrew). No verb is supplied in either colon — the Latin has none (Matos Soares 1932 adds 'serão' after 'mas'); see the decision 'nonsic'. 'a fácie terræ' → 'da face da terra' is also the Greek's plus, kept; fácies → face (glossary).
choices.1:5: Ídeo → 'Por isso'. in judício → 'no juízo' (D15 judícium → juízo; the study names this verse); the ambiguity reader heard the Last Judgment first and 'a judgment' second — judícium without an article is open in the same way. The second colon has no verb in the Latin and none is supplied (Matos Soares 1932 adds '(estarão)'); the reader noticed that 'ressurgirão' is the verb carried over, as resúrgent is in the Latin.
choices.1:6: novit → 'conhece' (a perfect with present sense); the ambiguity reader heard 'knows how the just live' before 'acknowledges and watches over' — novit is no narrower. períbit → 'perecerá': it is the way that perishes, the Latin's strange and exact image, left alone (DM1962 'leva à perda' explains it); the reader heard 'the wicked will end in destruction', which is what the image means.

audit.note: Latin = DO Psalm1.txt, seven prayed verses (1:1, 1:2, 1:3a, 1:3b, 1:4, 1:5, 1:6); 1:1 has a flex (†) and a mediant (*), the rest one '*' each. No titulus in DO's file (D7). The Hetzenauer 1914 print read was skipped overnight and is owed.

Psalm-level draft from consult/parallels/ps001.md. Vulgate-family support: Douay-Rheims and Matos Soares 1932 only. The Diurnal Monástico 1962 has this psalm; it is made from the Hebrew (scoffers, 'se compraz', 'não seca', 'ficarão de pé') and was used for diction only. DO's Portuguese was not used as evidence for anything (D12). Lewis & Short consulted for pestiléntia, decúrsus, beátus (letter B fetched into consult/). Septuagintal readings kept on purpose: cáthedra pestiléntiæ (1:1), the second 'non sic' and 'a fácie terræ' (1:4), resúrgent (1:5). No vós imperative in the psalm; God is not addressed in it, so the address question does not arise.

Draft 1: hard pass (ids and marks). Soft: 1:1 rhyme flagged at mediant and final (parou / sentou) — accepted in draft 1 as the Latin's own echo, mended in draft 2 after the stylist; 1:3a first colon +3 (mended in draft 2).
Draft 1 (prayed.v1.vos.json). Clean: no verse remarked; senses, images, the Latin's particular readings and every mark confirmed.

Draft 1. Five verses remarked; worst line 1:1, best 1:3b. Taken: 1:1 'se deteve' for 'parou' (the rhyme), 1:3a 'cursos de água', 1:5 'assembleia', 1:6 'caminho'. Refused and kept as options: 1:1 verb-last first colon and 'tomou assento', 1:4 the two copulas.

outcomes.remark: 'parou' / 'sentou' rhyme loudly between mediant and final → 'não se deteve'
'ímpios' is proparoxytone before the flex → 'que no conselho dos ímpios não andou'
outcomes.reason: The Latin's first colon is verb-first; 'ímpios' is two syllables in Brazilian speech (paroxytone by checks.py) and closes cola again in 1:4, so it cannot be avoided by reordering one colon. Recorded in the note of the ruling option.

outcomes.remark: close the verse with 'não tomou assento'
outcomes.reason: A ceremonious periphrasis for the plainest verb of the verse; with 'se deteve' at the mediant the rhyme it was meant to cure is already gone.

outcomes.remark: 'cursos das águas' sounds translated → 'cursos de água'
verbless opening is a calque → 'Não são assim os ímpios, não são assim'
outcomes.reason: The ellipsis is the Latin's figure, not a gap in the grammar; Matos Soares 1932 and the prayed Diurnal Monástico 1962 both print it verbless; two copulas put the colon four syllables over.

outcomes.remark: 'concílio' evokes a council of bishops → 'na assembleia dos justos'
'senda' is literary → 'o caminho dos ímpios'

audit.note: Draft 1, Portuguese only. Thirteen items and three unknown words (pestilência, concílio, senda). One real fault: 1:2 'a sua vontade' heard first as the Lord's will — mended by order (decision 'v2order'). Two unknown words dropped with the stylist's agreement (concílio, senda); 'pestilência' kept. The rest is the Latin's own openness, in nearly every case heard the right way first.

outcomes.remark: 'o homem': a male, or anyone
outcomes.reason: vir is the male and is prayed by everyone; 'homem' carries both, heard as 'anyone' first.

outcomes.remark: 'andou no conselho dos ímpios': followed their advice / frequented their council
outcomes.reason: consílium is both advice and a deliberating body; the Portuguese is as open as the Latin.

outcomes.remark: 'no caminho dos pecadores não parou': did not remain in their way of life / did not stop on a road they use
outcomes.reason: The figurative reading was heard first; the image is the Latin's.

outcomes.remark: 'cadeira da pestilência': a seat of moral contagion / a literally infected chair; 'pestilência' may be unknown
outcomes.reason: The Latin's image (a Septuagintal reading to be kept), heard rightly first; 'cadeira da peste' added as the plainer option and argued against.

outcomes.remark: 'na lei do Senhor está a sua vontade' heard first as the Lord's will expressed in the law
'na sua lei meditará': the man, or the Lord, meditates
outcomes.reason: Heard rightly (the man); the subject is in the verb ending in the Latin too.

outcomes.remark: 'no seu tempo': the tree's season / the man's appointed moment
outcomes.reason: suo is open in the same way; the tree's season was heard first.

outcomes.remark: 'prosperarão': turn out well / bring material success
'não ressurgirão no juízo': not come back to life at the Last Judgment / not reappear or stand at the judgment
outcomes.reason: Both are readings of resúrgent in judício, and the Latin's likelier one was heard first.

outcomes.remark: 'no juízo': the Last Judgment / a judgment
outcomes.reason: judícium without article is open in the same way.

outcomes.remark: second colon: the verb 'ressurgirão' carried over, or 'will have no place'
outcomes.reason: The Latin carries resúrgent over exactly so; no verb is supplied (rule 2).

outcomes.remark: 'conhece o caminho': knows how they live / acknowledges and watches over
'a senda dos ímpios perecerá': the way will vanish / the wicked will be destroyed; 'senda' may be unknown
outcomes.reason: 'senda' replaced by 'caminho'; the image of the way perishing is the Latin's and stays.

audit.note: v2. Wording changed against draft 1 in five verses: 1:1 'não se deteve' (was 'não parou'); 1:2 'Mas a sua vontade está na lei do Senhor' (order); 1:3a 'junto aos cursos de água' (was 'das águas'); 1:5 'na assembleia dos justos' (was 'no concílio'); 1:6 'o caminho dos ímpios' (was 'a senda'). All five are matters of order or of the plainer of two faithful words (D2); none changes a reading of the Latin. Draft 1 is prayed.v1.json (flat text prayed.v1.vos.json, the file the v1 critics read). Owed: the Hetzenauer 1914 print read of the Latin.

Draft 2: hard pass (ids and marks). No rhyme flag left. Soft: 1:1 flex colon +4 (15 against 11) — the price of 'não se deteve' for 'não parou'; accepted, since the flex half is recited on the tenor and the alternative is the rhyme the stylist refused ('parou' is one click away in the decision 'stetit'); 1:3a first colon still +3 by the checker, which does not elide 'de‿água' — accepted, nothing is added to the Latin.

Draft 2 (prayed.vos.json), run because five verses changed. Clean again: no verse remarked — sense, images, grammatical values and every mark confirmed, the reordered 1:2 and the merged via / iter of 1:6 included. The gate is clean.
